svg.aria-label: Diagram: what an Amazon Detective behaviour graph ingests, how it is built, and how its three volume limits behave on an unusual day. On sources, the Detective core package includes AWS CloudTrail logs, VPC Flow logs and GuardDuty findings, with two optional packages, EKS audit logs and AWS security findings from Security Hub CSPM, each of which can be started or stopped at any time. The ingestion design is deliberately independent of the customer's own logging: Detective consumes CloudTrail and VPC flow log events using independent and duplicative streams, and these processes do not affect or use the customer's existing CloudTrail and VPC flow log configurations, nor do they affect the performance of or increase costs for those services. Two good properties follow: an attacker who can edit a trail cannot blind Detective, and the customer is not billed twice for the same records. The flow log ingestion has documented exclusions that matter for coverage, because Detective ingests flow logs produced by Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud instances running in those VPCs only, and no other resources such as NAT gateways, RDS instances or Fargate clusters are used; it ingests both IPv4 and IPv6 records but not MAC records produced by Elastic Fabric Adapters; and it ingests records only when the value of the log-status field is in OK state. For a Fargate-heavy estate the network half of the graph is therefore largely empty, and an empty result looks exactly like a clean one. Data is retained for up to one year per source package, there is a 30-day free trial per Region, and stopping then restarting an optional source leaves a permanent gap because Detective does not retroactively ingest data on restart. The central argument is that three documented limits all bind hardest at the volume an incident produces. First, the training period. Detective's main investigative move is comparison, since one avenue of investigation is to compare activity during the finding scope time to activity before the finding was detected, on the principle that activity not seen before might be more likely to be suspicious; several profile panels display a baseline value showing average activity during the 45 days before the scope time; and to build that picture Detective needs access to at least two weeks of data. The first two weeks after activation are a training period, during which the comparison panels display a message saying so. Because Detective is usually enabled during or just after an incident, the panels it was opened for will often report they are in training, and nothing retroactively creates the missing baseline. Analysis maturity also increases with the number of accounts in the graph. Second, the high-volume entity cap. When an entity has too many relationships in a time period Detective cannot store them all; it maintains a limit on connections per time interval, and if an entity exceeds that limit it discards the connections for that interval. The same page states that a high-volume time interval might itself be an indicator of suspicious activity, so the condition causing the discard is a thing worth investigating. Detective handles this openly: it notifies on the profile, lists the affected relationships and intervals, and offers to set scope time to a high-volume interval, with that navigation starting 30 days before the interval. AWS offers an alternative line of investigation rather than a recovery, hedged as you might be able to analyze that activity based on the entity at the other end of the relationship, because while an EC2 instance might be connected to from millions of IP addresses, a single IP address connects to far fewer EC2 instances. An individual IP address may therefore have fewer relationships than the affected instance, leaving useful connections visible, but this does not guarantee recovery of every discarded relationship. Third, the volume quotas. Above 10 TB per day an administrator account cannot enable Detective; above 10 TB per day no new member account can be added to the graph; and above 15 TB per day Detective stops ingesting data, a ceiling 50 percent above the enablement quota. AWS states the 15 TB per day quota reflects both normal data volume and spikes in it, so it is not a spike allowance on top of normal running. Suspension fails safe, since no new data is ingested but existing data is not removed and remains usable, and the console shows a message. Recovery requires working with Support, and the documented way to speed that up is to remove member accounts to get below the quota first, which is an awkward remedy mid-incident. Detective checks the volume daily and warns on the console as the quota approaches, so the condition is observable in advance and deserves an alarm. On construction, extraction is deterministic and based on configured mapping rules, while analytics run more complex algorithms that look for API calls an entity does not normally use and for large spikes in call volume, both of which are statements about normality and therefore depend on the training period. The recommended actions are to enable Detective organisation-wide before it is needed and treat the first fortnight as installation rather than service, to alarm on distance from the 15 TB ceiling instead of waiting for a console message, to try the opposite end of a relationship when a high-volume notice appears, without assuming it restores what was discarded, and to know what fraction of compute is Fargate because that is the fraction of network activity missing from the graph.
svg.title: Three documented limits, all of them tightest on the day an investigation starts
svg.text: A tool for unusual days, with three limits indexed to how unusual the day is.
Amazon Detective — none of this is hidden. It is all written down, and it all points the same way.
WHAT GOES IN
core CloudTrail · VPC flow logs · GuardDuty
optional EKS audit logs · Security Hub CSPM findings
“independent and duplicative streams” that “do not affect
or use your existing” config — and cost you nothing extra.
An attacker who can edit your trail still cannot blind it.
WHAT DOES NOT
Flow logs from “EC2 instances… only”.
no NAT gateways · no RDS · no Fargate
Not EFA MAC records. Only log-status = OK.
Run on Fargate and the network half is empty —
and an empty result looks exactly like a clean one.
Three limits. The day your volume spikes is the day an entity goes high-volume is the day somebody is doing something.
1 · It needs a fortnight first
“Detective needs access to at least
two weeks of data”. Panels compare
against the “45 days before”.
“The first two weeks… are a
training period.”
You enable it during the incident.
The panels say they are in training.
Nothing creates the history later.
2 · It drops the busy interval
“If an entity exceeds that limit, then
Detective discards the connections
for that time interval.”
Same page: “A high-volume time
interval might be an indicator of
suspicious activity.”
It tells you, and lists them. The IP
side “might” help. No guarantee.
3 · Above 15 TB it stops
>10 TB/day cannot enable
>10 TB/day cannot add a member
>15 TB/day STOPS INGESTING
“reflects both normal data volume
and spikes” — not a spike allowance.
“you must work with Support to get
it re-enabled”
First, remove member accounts.
What makes these limits rather than traps: every one of them is announced
High-volume → a notice, a list of intervals, and a button to scope to one. Quota → a console warning on approach.
Training → the affected panels say so themselves. Suspension fails safe: “existing data is not removed”.
Three questions, before the day you need it
How long has the graph run, over how many accounts? — under two weeks or one account and the comparisons are not ready.
What is today's volume, and how far from 15 TB? — if nobody knows, that is the first alarm to build.
What fraction of compute is Fargate? — that is the fraction of network activity the graph does not have.
Nothing here is a defect. The limits are correlated, and the only way to see it is to read three pages together.
